stages.sub: Who gains and who loses when a firm charges different prices to different groups of customers.

steps.q: A rail firm splits peak-time commuters (who have no other way to get to work) from leisure travellers (who could drive or go another day). Commuters barely change their travel if price rises. Which group is this?
steps.right: The group with less responsive demand
steps.wrong: The group with more responsive demand
steps.hint: Think about how much their quantity bought changes when price changes.

steps.q: Leisure travellers cut their trips a lot if the price goes up, since they have other options. Which group is this?
steps.right: The group with more responsive demand
steps.wrong: The group with less responsive demand
steps.hint: How much does their quantity bought change when price changes?

steps.q: To keep the two groups separate, the firm has to check tickets, ages or booking times so no one buys at the cheaper price and resells it. Does running this checking system cost the firm anything?
steps.right: Yes, it uses up money and staff time
steps.wrong: No, splitting customers is free once prices are set
steps.hint: Someone has to design the rules, check them and stop people cheating the system.

steps.q: The rail firm charges commuters a higher price than leisure travellers. What happens to the amount of surplus commuters keep, compared with paying one uniform price?
steps.right: It falls, since they now pay more for the same journeys
steps.wrong: It rises, since they get priority booking
steps.hint: They are paying more than before for the same trips. What does that do to the gap between what they'd pay and what they do pay?

steps.q: Overall the firm collects more revenue from the group willing to pay more, while only facing the extra checking costs. What happens to the firm's profit compared with charging one price to everyone?
steps.right: Profit rises, and some of it can fund future investment
steps.wrong: Profit falls once the extra costs are paid
